decisions.question: How does the Next.js frontend reach the FastAPI backend, and how is the session cookie scoped?
options: Next.js Route Handlers proxy all API calls server-side to FastAPI (browser only ever talks to the Next.js origin; cookie is HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Lax, scoped to the Next.js origin)
Browser calls FastAPI directly, cross-origin (requires CORS with credentials, SameSite=None; Secure cookies, HTTPS even in local dev)
decisions.proposed_default: Next.js Route Handlers proxy all API calls server-side to FastAPI (browser only ever talks to the Next.js origin; cookie is HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Lax, scoped to the Next.js origin)
decisions.chosen: Next.js Route Handlers proxy all API calls server-side to FastAPI (browser only ever talks to the Next.js origin; cookie is HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Lax, scoped to the Next.js origin)
decisions.rules_out: Direct cross-origin browser-to-FastAPI calls; CORS-with-credentials configuration; SameSite=None cookies; any requirement for HTTPS in local/dev compose to keep cookies working.
decisions.rationale: Keeps cookies same-site, avoids CORS, and fits NFR-5's single-compose-stack posture. The two contract shapes are documented in api-contracts.md.

decisions.question: Are sessions DB-backed or a stateless JWT?
options: DB-backed sessions table (id, user_id, expires_at, created_at, revoked_at)
Stateless JWT with a server-side denylist table for revocation
decisions.proposed_default: DB-backed sessions table (id, user_id, expires_at, created_at, revoked_at)
decisions.chosen: DB-backed sessions table (id, user_id, expires_at, created_at, revoked_at)
decisions.rules_out: Stateless JWT issuance; any client-held bearer token not tied to a server-side revocable row.
decisions.rationale: FR-7 requires sign-out to invalidate the session server-side. A stateless JWT cannot satisfy that without a denylist table, which is strictly more machinery than a sessions table for no benefit here.

decisions.question: Is link delete a hard delete or a soft delete?
options: Soft delete: deleted_at column on links, unique constraint on code across all rows (deleted or not)
Hard delete: row removed, code uniqueness enforced only among live rows, plus a separate reserved-codes mechanism to prevent reissue
decisions.proposed_default: Soft delete: deleted_at column on links, unique constraint on code across all rows (deleted or not)
decisions.chosen: Soft delete: deleted_at column on links, unique constraint on code across all rows (deleted or not)
decisions.rules_out: Hard-deleting link rows; any separate reserved-codes table or bookkeeping structure to prevent code reissue after deletion.
decisions.rationale: FR-5 requires the code is never reissued. A unique constraint on code across all rows (including soft-deleted ones) guarantees that without a second structure.

decisions.question: What CSRF mitigation strategy applies to state-changing endpoints?
options: SameSite=Lax cookies plus same-origin-only route handlers (no separate CSRF token)
Double-submit CSRF token issued and validated on every state-changing request
decisions.proposed_default: SameSite=Lax cookies plus same-origin-only route handlers (no separate CSRF token)
decisions.chosen: SameSite=Lax cookies plus same-origin-only route handlers (no separate CSRF token)
decisions.rules_out: A separate CSRF token issuance/validation mechanism.
decisions.rationale: Given D-1's proxy topology, requests are same-site by construction. SameSite=Lax blocks cross-site submissions from attaching the cookie, closing CSRF without extra token machinery.
